title: Ch 2 · NMOS and PMOS structure, and channel formation (Figs. 2.2–2.8)
subtitle: Press ▶ to build the devices · tap a part · Explode lifts the gates
steps: The p-type substrate is the body (bulk) of all NMOS devices
An n-well gives the PMOS device its own local substrate
Heavily doped regions make the source and the drain of each device
A thin gate oxide and a polysilicon gate go on top. L and W are the gate dimensions
Metal contacts give the terminals: S, G, D and B (bulk or well)
NMOS, VG > 0: the gate pushes holes away. A depletion region with negative ions remains
NMOS, VGS > VTH: electrons make an inversion channel from S to D
PMOS, VGS more negative than −|VTH|: holes make the PMOS channel

objects.label: p-substrate
objects.info: The p-type substrate is the body (bulk) of each NMOS device. Engineers connect it to the most negative supply. Then the S/D junction diodes stay in reverse bias (p. 11).

objects.label: n-well
objects.info: The n-well is a local n-type substrate for the PMOS device. Engineers connect it to the most positive supply. Each PMOS device can have its own well (p. 12).

objects.label: n+ source
objects.info: A heavily doped n-type region. The source gives the electrons to the channel (p. 11).

objects.label: n+ drain
objects.info: A heavily doped n-type region. The drain collects the electrons. The NMOS structure is symmetric, so the source and the drain can change roles (p. 11).

objects.label: p+ source
objects.info: A heavily doped p-type region in the n-well. In a PMOS device, the source gives holes to the channel.

objects.label: p+ drain
objects.info: A heavily doped p-type region in the n-well. It collects the holes.

objects.label: p+ bulk tap
objects.info: A p+ region gives an ohmic (low-resistance) connection to the p-substrate (Fig. 2.3).

objects.label: n+ well tap
objects.info: An n+ region gives an ohmic connection to the n-well.

objects.label: gate oxide
objects.info: A thin layer of silicon dioxide (SiO2). It insulates the gate from the substrate. Its thickness is tox. For tox = 50 Å, Cox is approximately 6.9 fF/µm² (p. 14).

objects.label: poly gate
objects.info: The gate is polysilicon with heavy doping. Its dimension along the S–D path is the length L. Its dimension across is the width W (p. 11).

objects.label: PMOS gate
objects.info: The PMOS gate is the same as the NMOS gate. All polarities are opposite.

objects.label: L
objects.info: L: the gate length, along the path from source to drain.

objects.label: W
objects.info: W: the gate width, perpendicular to the length.

objects.label: S
objects.info: NMOS source terminal.

objects.label: G
objects.info: NMOS gate terminal.

objects.label: D
objects.info: NMOS drain terminal.

objects.label: B
objects.info: NMOS bulk terminal. All NMOS devices share this substrate (p. 12).

objects.label: S
objects.info: PMOS source terminal. In the PMOS symbol, the source is on top, because it has the higher voltage (p. 12).

objects.label: G
objects.info: PMOS gate terminal.

objects.label: D
objects.info: PMOS drain terminal.

objects.label: B
objects.info: PMOS bulk terminal: the n-well contact. It usually connects to VDD.

objects.label: depletion region
objects.info: The positive gate pushes the holes away. Negative ions remain, and they mirror the gate charge. No carriers are free here, so no current flows yet (Fig. 2.6b).

objects.label: electron channel
objects.info: When VGS is more than VTH, electrons come from the source. They make an inversion layer under the oxide. The layer connects S and D, so the device is on (Fig. 2.6d).
With a positive VDS, electrons move from S to D. The current ID flows from D to S.

objects.label: PMOS depletion
objects.info: A negative gate pushes the electrons of the n-well away. Positive ions remain.

objects.label: hole channel
objects.info: When VGS is sufficiently negative, holes make the inversion layer. The PMOS device is then on (Fig. 2.8).
